---
title: "07 — Linear Algebra over Finite Fields"
---

## Coordinates you can eliminate

Three contest situations, apparently unrelated:

- You may XOR together any subset of $n$ given numbers. Which values are
  reachable, and how many ways is each one reachable?
- Count the spanning trees of a weighted graph, modulo a prime.
- A sequence is defined by a huge state machine, and you need its
  $10^{18}$-th term.

All three become easy the moment the objects are written as **vectors** and
the problem is attacked with **reversible row operations**. Subsets of XORs
are a vector space over the two-element field; spanning trees are a
determinant; a finite-dimensional transition forces a linear recurrence you
can exponentiate.

One warning before anything else, because it invalidates more solutions than
any other mistake here: **name the scalar domain first.** Real numbers,
$\mathbb F_p$, and $\mathbb F_2$ support the same algebra but have completely
different hazards, and a composite modulus is not a field at all — Gaussian
elimination can silently produce a wrong answer there.

## Prerequisites and learning objectives

Read [proofs and invariants](../00-foundations/chapter.qmd) and
[fields and units](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd); the recurrence sections
also use [polynomial division](../06-polynomials/chapter.qmd).

You should finish able to count solutions from a rank, prove why XOR
representations are uniformly distributed, turn a spanning-tree count into a
determinant, and explain why a finite-dimensional transition yields a linear
recurrence. Your library supplies elimination and polynomial arithmetic; this
chapter supplies the meaning and the preconditions.

## 1. Vectors, coordinates, and reversible equations

Fix a field $K$. A vector in $K^c$ is a list of $c$ field elements, added and
scaled coordinatewise. A **linear combination** of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is
$\sum_i a_iv_i$; their **span** is the set of all such combinations. A list is
**independent** when the only combination equal to zero has all coefficients
zero. A **basis** is an independent spanning list, and its length is the
**dimension**.

Why a basis is worth having: $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ form a basis of $K^2$, and
$(x,y) = (x-y)(1,0) + y(1,1)$ — *uniquely*. Uniqueness is automatic: two
different coefficient lists for the same vector would subtract to a nonzero
dependence. So a basis is a lossless coordinate system, the linear-algebra
analogue of compressing a DP state down to its genuinely independent
parameters.

A matrix $A \in K^{r\times c}$ encodes the map $x \mapsto Ax$. Its **kernel**
is $\{x : Ax = 0\}$, its **image** is $\{Ax\}$, and the dimension of the image
is the **rank**. Solving $Ax = b$ asks whether $b$ is in the image, and if so
for all preimages.

### Elimination, and the count it produces

Row operations do not change the solution set, because each one replaces an
equation by an equivalent combination of equations — and each is reversible
(undo a swap, divide by the nonzero scalar, subtract back the added row).

Run the usual loop: maintain a pivot row, and for each column find a nonzero
entry, swap it up, normalize, eliminate the rest. The invariant after
processing a column is that every pivot column has a single leading entry and
all later rows are zero in earlier pivot columns — which is what guarantees no
equation is lost and each pivot pins down exactly one new variable.

The number of pivots is $\operatorname{rank}(A)$. After elimination:

- a zero row with a nonzero augmented entry means the system is
  **inconsistent**;
- otherwise there are $c - \operatorname{rank}(A)$ **free** variables, and
  every assignment of them extends to exactly one solution (solve the pivot
  variables backwards).

Over $\mathbb F_q$ that gives exactly $q^{\,c-\operatorname{rank}(A)}$
solutions; over an infinite field, a solution set of that dimension. The same
argument with $b = 0$ is the **rank–nullity identity**
$\dim\ker A = c - \operatorname{rank}(A)$. And if $x_0$ is any solution, every
solution is $x_0 + z$ with $z \in \ker A$, since $A(x - x_0) = 0$: the
solution set is a translated subspace, an **affine space** — note it usually
does not contain $0$.

::: {.callout-note title="Rank counts equations, not rows"}
Over $\mathbb F_5$, the system $x+y+z = 2$, $2x+2y+2z = 4$ has two rows but
rank one. Pick $y,z$ freely and set $x = 2-y-z$: $5^{3-1} = 25$ solutions.

Change the second right-hand side to $3$ and the system becomes
*inconsistent* — not rank two. Subtracting twice the first row leaves
$0 = 3 - 4 = 4 \ne 0$ in $\mathbb F_5$.
:::

Dense elimination costs $O(rc\min(r,c))$. For a **determinant**, do not
normalize the pivot row: instead multiply the running answer by each pivot,
negate on each row swap, and eliminate using the ratio to the pivot.

::: {.callout-warning title="Composite moduli are not fields"}
A nonzero entry modulo a composite number need not be invertible, so
elimination may divide by a non-unit and lose solutions. Modulo $6$, the
equation $2x = 2$ has solutions $x = 1$ and $x = 4$; "dividing by $2$" reports
one. Rank-based counting formulas do not apply. Use prime-factor methods,
fraction-free (Bareiss) elimination, or exact integer algorithms.
:::

### What the determinant is

For an $n\times n$ matrix,

$$\det A = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{n}A_{i,\sigma(i)},$$

where the sign is $(-1)^{\#\text{inversions}}$. Each summand picks one entry
from every row and every column. From this definition: swapping two rows flips
the sign; adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing (the extra
terms cancel in pairs with repeated rows); and a triangular matrix has
determinant equal to its diagonal product. Those three facts are exactly what
make the elimination procedure above valid.

Over a field, $\det A \ne 0$ iff every column has a pivot, iff $Ax = b$ has a
unique solution for every $b$. The permutation definition also makes sense
over any commutative ring, even when division-based elimination does not. The
empty matrix has determinant $1$.

## 2. XOR basis: elimination over $\mathbb F_2$

A machine word is a vector of bits, and XOR is vector addition — so "which
values can I reach by XORing a subset?" is the span of a set of vectors over
$\mathbb F_2$, and Gaussian elimination applies verbatim.

Keep at most one basis vector per leading (highest set) bit. To insert a word,
XOR away the leading bits you already have; if something remains, it is a new
independent direction, and if nothing remains the word was already in the
span. Insertion costs $O(B)$ for $B$-bit words.

With rank $r$ from $n$ inputs:

- the span has exactly $2^r$ distinct values;
- every reachable value has exactly $2^{\,n-r}$ subsets producing it.

*Why the representations are uniform:* the map from a subset (a vector in
$\mathbb F_2^n$) to the XOR it produces is linear with rank $r$, so its kernel
has $2^{n-r}$ elements, and every nonempty fiber is a translate of the kernel.
Concretely, for the words $1, 2, 3$ the rank is $2$, and each of $0,1,2,3$ has
two representations — zero comes from the empty subset *and* from all three
words.

**Getting the $k$-th smallest span value** ($0 \le k < 2^r$) requires more
than a triangular basis: fully reduce, so each pivot bit appears in only one
basis vector, sort by increasing pivot bit, and XOR the vectors selected by
the bits of $k$. Then the numeric order of results matches the order of
coefficient masks, because two masks first differ at some pivot bit, and lower
basis vectors cannot touch that bit. Failure case: the triangular vectors
$1, 3$ in pivot order enumerate $0, 1, 3, 2$ — not sorted. Reducing $3$ by $1$
gives the basis $1, 2$, which does enumerate in order.

### Recognition: XOR on graphs

Root a DFS tree and give each vertex its XOR distance `dist[v]` from the root.
Each non-tree edge $(u,v,w)$ contributes the cycle value
`dist[u] ^ w ^ dist[v]`. Then for $s, t$ in the same undirected component, the
set of XORs of **walks** from $s$ to $t$ is

$$\texttt{dist[s]} \oplus \texttt{dist[t]} \;+\; \operatorname{span}(\text{cycle values of that component}).$$

*Proof sketch.* XOR any walk with the fixed tree path from $s$ to $t$: every
vertex now has even edge-incidence, so the remaining edge multiset decomposes
into cycles, and each cycle is a combination of the fundamental cycles.
Conversely, to realize any cycle value, walk to the cycle along tree edges,
go around, and come back the same way — the connector edges appear twice and
cancel.

::: {.callout-warning title="Walks, not simple paths"}
The statement is about walks. A triangle hanging off the $s$–$t$ path can be
inserted into a *walk*, but a simple path cannot enter and leave it through a
single articulation vertex. If a problem says "simple path", this
characterization does not apply.
:::

Building all component bases costs $O((n+m)B)$ time. Never reuse one
component's cycle space for endpoints in another component.

## 3. Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem

Spanning trees are combinatorial objects with no obvious algebraic form, yet
their total weight is a single determinant. Form the **Laplacian** of a
weighted undirected graph:

$$L_{ii} = \sum_{j \ne i}w_{ij}, \qquad L_{ij} = -w_{ij}\ (i \ne j),$$

adding parallel-edge weights first. Delete any one row and the matching
column; the determinant of the remaining $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix equals the
sum over spanning trees of the product of their edge weights.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why it is true"}
Orient each edge arbitrarily and let $B$ be the incidence matrix: each column
has $+1$ at one endpoint and $-1$ at the other. With $W$ the diagonal matrix
of edge weights, $L = BWB^{T}$ — an edge contributes its weight to both
diagonal entries and its negative to the two off-diagonal ones. Delete the
root row from $B$ to get $\bar B$.

The **Cauchy–Binet** expansion of a determinant of a product gives

$$\det(\bar B W \bar B^{T}) = \sum_{\substack{S \subseteq E\\ |S| = n-1}}\det(\bar B_{[:,S]})^2\prod_{e \in S}w_e .$$

Now classify the subsets $S$. If $S$ contains a cycle, its incidence columns
are dependent and the determinant is $0$. If $S$ is disconnected, some
component avoids the deleted root and its rows sum to zero — again $0$. If $S$
is a spanning tree, repeatedly remove a non-root leaf and expand along its
single entry, reaching the empty matrix with determinant $\pm 1$; squaring
kills the sign. Only spanning trees survive, each with its weight product.
:::

**Directed versions need a convention, and getting it backwards is a classic
bug.** With out-degree on the diagonal,
$L_{ii} = \sum_{i \to j} w_{ij}$ and $L_{ij} = -\sum_{i \to j}w_{ij}$, the
root cofactor counts arborescences pointing **toward** the root. For trees
pointing **away**, use the in-degree convention
$L_{ii} = \sum_{j \to i}w_{ji}$, $L_{ij} = -\sum_{j\to i}w_{ji}$. Test on the
single-edge graph $r \to v$: deleting $r$'s row and column gives determinant
$1$ only under the in-degree convention, matching the unique tree pointing
away from $r$. Two vertices are enough to catch a transposed matrix.

**Checks.** A unit-weight triangle leaves
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $3$ — the three
trees obtained by deleting one edge. With weights $a, b, c$ the cofactor is
$ab+ac+bc$; for $(2,3,5)$ it is $31$.

Cost is $O(n^3)$ by dense elimination. Parallel edges add their weights;
self-loops contribute nothing. Under a modulus you get the count modulo that
modulus — and a **zero determinant does not certify disconnection**, it may be
a genuine count that happens to be divisible by the prime (as $31$ is, modulo
$31$).

## 4. Linear recurrences: reduce $x^N$, don't multiply matrices

Suppose $s_n = c_1s_{n-1} + \cdots + c_ks_{n-k}$ holds for every $n \ge k$,
with $s_0,\ldots,s_{k-1}$ given in a commutative ring. The polynomial

$$C(x) = x^k - c_1x^{k-1} - \cdots - c_k$$

*annihilates* the sequence: it encodes "replace $x^k$ by the combination of
lower powers". So reduce $x^N$ modulo $C$; the remainder's coefficients tell
you exactly how to combine $s_0, \ldots, s_{k-1}$ to get $s_N$.

*Why this is legitimate,* rather than a suggestive coincidence: define the
linear functional $\Lambda(x^j) = s_j$, extended linearly. The recurrence says
precisely $\Lambda(x^jC(x)) = 0$ for all $j \ge 0$. Writing
$x^N = Q(x)C(x) + R(x)$ with $\deg R < k$ and applying $\Lambda$ gives
$s_N = \Lambda(R)$. Note that dividing by the *monic* $C$ uses no inverses, so
this works even modulo a composite number — unlike most of this chapter.

*Concretely:* for Fibonacci, $C(x) = x^2 - x - 1$, and
$x^5 \equiv 5x + 3$, so every sequence with this recurrence satisfies
$s_5 = 3s_0 + 5s_1$. (Fibonacci: $3\cdot 0 + 5 \cdot 1 = 5$. ✓)

Binary exponentiation with reduction after each step costs $O(k^2\log N)$ ring
operations (Kitamasa) and $O(k)$ memory; NTT-based products or Bostan–Mori do
better for large $k$. This replaces $k\times k$ matrix power, which is
$O(k^3\log N)$.

### Discovering the recurrence: Berlekamp–Massey

Often you can compute a prefix of the sequence but do not know the
recurrence. Berlekamp–Massey maintains the *shortest* recurrence consistent
with the prefix read so far.

Its central quantity is the **discrepancy**: the actual next term minus the
one predicted by the current recurrence. Zero discrepancy means the prefix
extends for free. A nonzero discrepancy is a new independent constraint; the
algorithm cancels it by subtracting a shifted copy of a *saved* earlier
recurrence that had nonzero discrepancy, scaled by the ratio of the two
discrepancies. The shift is what keeps all previously satisfied constraints
intact, and the saved state comes from the last time the required order
increased. That ratio is also why the algorithm needs a field.

Contract: $O(T^2)$ field operations and $O(T)$ space on a prefix of $T$ terms
(often stated as $O(TL)$ for linear complexity $L$).

**How many terms are enough?** If the sequence genuinely has shortest
recurrence order $L$ valid from index $L$, then $2L$ terms determine it. One
argument: such a sequence has a rational generating function with denominator
degree $\le L$ and numerator degree $< L$; two such functions agreeing through
degree $2L-1$ give a cross-multiplied numerator of degree $< 2L$ with $2L$
leading zero coefficients, hence zero. (The all-zero sequence has order zero.)

**But no finite prefix proves anything about an unknown future** — the
sequence $0,0,0,0,1,\ldots$ defeats any inference from its first four terms.
Establish that a recurrence *exists*, with a bound on its order, before
extrapolating. The next subsection is how you usually do that.

### Matrices and Cayley–Hamilton

The **characteristic polynomial** is $\chi_A(x) = \det(xI - A)$; the
**minimal polynomial** $m_A$ is the monic polynomial of least degree with
$m_A(A) = 0$. Cayley–Hamilton says $\chi_A(A) = 0$.

A clean way to see it: the cofactor identity
$(xI - A)\operatorname{adj}(xI-A) = \chi_A(x)I$, compared coefficient by
coefficient in $x$ and then multiplied by successive powers of $A$,
telescopes to $\chi_A(A) = 0$. (This avoids simply "substituting $x = A$",
which is not a valid step for matrix-coefficient polynomials.)

The consequence you use in contests: for any vectors $u, v$, the scalar
sequence $u^{T}A^{n}v$ satisfies a linear recurrence of order at most the
matrix dimension — so if your DP is a fixed linear transition on $d$ states,
any observed scalar sequence has order $\le d$, and Berlekamp–Massey on $2d$
terms is justified.

The observed order can be *smaller*: for
$A = \operatorname{diag}(2,3)$ with $u = v = (1,0)^T$, the sequence is $2^n$,
order one, even though $\chi_A = (x-2)(x-3)$.

## 5. Characteristic polynomials and black-box methods

For a dense matrix over a field, similarity $A \mapsto S^{-1}AS$ preserves
$\det(xI - A)$. **Hessenberg reduction** uses paired row/column operations —
the column operation is the inverse of the row operation, which is what
preserves the characteristic polynomial — to zero everything below the first
subdiagonal in $O(n^3)$. For upper Hessenberg $H$, the leading minors
$D_i = \det(xI_i - H_{1:i,1:i})$, with $D_0 = 1$, satisfy

$$D_i = (x - h_{ii})D_{i-1} - \sum_{k=1}^{i-1}h_{ki}\left(\prod_{j=k}^{i-1}h_{j+1,j}\right)D_{k-1}.$$

Expanding the last column, a non-diagonal choice forces the whole intervening
subdiagonal chain and leaves the leading minor of size $k-1$ — which is why no
minors are missing. Accumulating the polynomials costs $O(n^3)$ overall. The
alternative — computing determinants at $n+1$ points and interpolating — costs
$O(n^4)$ naively and needs a field with enough points.

For a huge **sparse** matrix, dense elimination wastes work on zeros.
**Wiedemann's** method picks random $u, v$, generates $a_i = u^{T}A^{i}v$, and
runs Berlekamp–Massey on it. The scalar sequence's minimal polynomial divides
the matrix's, and random projection makes them equal with high probability.
Generating $2n$ terms costs $O(n\mathcal V + n^2)$, where $\mathcal V$ is one
matrix-vector product.

Assumptions and failure modes, which matter because this is a randomized
black box:

- A projection can miss invariant factors; repeat with fresh randomness.
- Over a small field you may need an extension field and a proved projection
  strategy. Switching primes changes the problem, and helps only when integer
  reconstruction was the goal.
- It pays off only when one matrix-vector multiply is genuinely fast;
  otherwise prefer dense elimination.
- Getting a *determinant* out needs more than the scalar recurrence: use a
  proven preconditioning recipe and account for the preconditioner's own
  determinant.
- Testing a returned annihilator on extra random vectors has an error
  probability; a deterministic certificate requires checking a spanning set.

## 6. Common pitfalls

- Dividing modulo a composite number silently invalidates elimination.
- Floating-point partial pivoting is about numerical stability; "largest
  pivot" has no meaning in a finite field, and no pivoting rule repairs an
  ill-conditioned *model*.
- A determinant flips sign on every row swap — track it.
- A graph XOR basis is built from cycle values, not raw edge weights.
- Kirchhoff treats parallel edges separately; merging them without adding
  weights changes the answer.
- Berlekamp–Massey sign and ordering conventions differ between templates.
  Verify yours on Fibonacci before the contest, not during it.

## 7. Practice, in order

1. **Application — [Xor Sum 3, AtCoder ABC141 F](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc141/tasks/abc141_f)**. XOR basis after transforming the objective.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Bits set in the XOR of all numbers contribute a fixed amount.
   2. Mask those bits away from every vector.
   3. Maximize a subset XOR on the remaining bits and relate the two groups.
   </details>

2. **Synthesis — [Spices, AtCoder ABC236 F](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc236/tasks/abc236_f)**. Minimum-weight basis and an exchange argument.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Being able to create every mask means selecting a full-rank basis.
   2. Sort candidates by cost.
   3. Insert a vector exactly when it raises the XOR-basis rank (matroid greedy).
   </details>

3. **Synthesis — [Xor-matic Number of the Graph, CF 724G](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/724/G)**. Cycle space and aggregate counting.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. DFS XOR distances make each non-tree edge a cycle vector.
   2. For a bit represented in the cycle basis, exactly half of the span values contain it.
   3. Otherwise its contribution depends only on endpoint distance bits; sum per component.
   </details>

## Exercises and solution workshop

### 1. Concept check: a fiber count

Over $\mathbb F_3$, how many triples satisfy $x+y+z = 1$ and $x + 2y = 0$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Choose one coordinate freely and count the completions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The second equation gives $x = y$ (since $2 = -1$), and the first then gives
$z = 1 + y$. Three solutions, one per value of $y$ — matching
$3^{\,3-2} = 3$, since the two rows are independent.

Note the solution set is a *translate* of the kernel, not a subspace: the zero
vector does not satisfy the first equation.
:::

### 2. Application: a partition objective

Given nonnegative $B$-bit words, split them into two groups to maximize the
sum of the two group XORs — the reduction behind ABC141 F.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Let $T$ be the XOR of all inputs and examine one bit of
$X + (T \oplus X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At a bit where $T$ is set, exactly one group has it, contributing a fixed
amount. At a bit where $T$ is clear, the groups agree, so the bit contributes
twice if $X$ has it. Hence the objective is

$$T + 2\,(X \mathbin{\&} \lnot T),$$

with the complement restricted to the $B$ input bits.

So mask every input by $\lnot T$ and maximize the subset XOR with a basis,
greedily improving from the highest pivot down. Cost $O(nB)$ time, $O(B)$
space. For inputs $3, 6, 5$: $T = 0$, the maximum masked XOR is $6$, and the
answer is $12$. Maximizing the *unmasked* $X$ would waste effort optimizing
bits whose contribution is already fixed.

Edge case: if both groups must be nonempty and $n \ge 2$, an optimum with
positive masked XOR is automatically proper; if the maximum is zero every
partition attains $T$, so any proper one works.
:::

### 3. Synthesis: a cheapest basis

Prove that sorting vectors by nonnegative cost and accepting each one exactly
when it raises the rank yields a cheapest basis of the span.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Exchange one vector of an optimal basis when greedy accepts its next vector.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Maintain the invariant that some optimal basis contains the greedy prefix
accepted so far. When greedy accepts $v$, write $v$ in that optimal basis.
Since $v$ is independent of the prefix, some $w$ with nonzero coefficient lies
outside the prefix. Swapping $w$ for $v$ still gives a basis, because the same
expression solves for $w$.

Moreover $w$ cannot be a vector greedy rejected earlier — rejected vectors lie
in the prefix span — so $w$ comes later in cost order and
$\operatorname{cost}(w) \ge \operatorname{cost}(v)$. The exchange therefore
does not increase the total, and the invariant survives. (This is the matroid
greedy argument.)

Cost $O(n\log n + nB)$ for XOR vectors. With costs $c_1 = 4$, $c_2 = 5$,
$c_3 = 3$, greedy accepts vectors $3$ then $1$ for total $7$; processing in
index order would pick the more expensive pair.
:::

### 4. Advanced: a modular determinant is not a certificate

A triangle has edge weights $2, 3, 5$. Count its weighted spanning trees
modulo $31$. Does the result certify that the graph is disconnected?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Enumerate which edge is deleted.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three trees weigh $2\cdot 3$, $2 \cdot 5$, and $3 \cdot 5$, totalling
$31$ — so the determinant is $0$ modulo $31$ even though the graph is
connected.

Exact counting and residue-field computation answer different questions. Any
determinant used as a randomized existence certificate needs its own error
analysis; see
[algebraic graph methods](../18-algebraic-graph-methods/chapter.qmd).
:::

## Contest checklist and reference sheet

- Identify the scalar field or ring before choosing a routine.
- Say out loud what the columns, the equations, or the bit coordinates
  represent.
- Count independent parameters; do not confuse the number of solutions with
  the number of distinct images.
- Check whether the statement is about walks, simple paths, or trees.
- Prove a recurrence exists (and bound its order) before extrapolating a
  sampled prefix.
- Verify determinant signs, orientation conventions, and the empty/zero case.

| Object | Result | Contract and cost |
|---|---|---|
| Consistent $Ax = b$ | $q^{\,c-\operatorname{rank}A}$ solutions | field $\mathbb F_q$; dense $O(rc\min(r,c))$ |
| XOR span of rank $r$ | $2^r$ values, $2^{\,n-r}$ representations each | $B$-bit inputs; $O(nB)$ |
| Weighted spanning trees | a Laplacian principal cofactor | $O(n^3)$ elimination; self-loops excluded |
| Order-$k$ recurrence | reduce $x^N$ by its monic polynomial | any commutative ring; $O(k^2\log N)$ |
| Observed matrix sequence | order at most $n$ | $u^TA^jv$; projection can hide directions |
